🔔 Kalshi ruling puts CFTC prediction rules at risk 

⚠️ A federal appeals court ruled on Aug. 28 that Kalshi had not shown Nevada’s regulation of its sports-event contracts was likely preempted by federal commodities law. The unanimous decision allows Nevada gaming authorities to enforce state requirements while litigation continues.

⚠️ Kalshi argued that its sports-event contracts qualified as swaps under the Commodity Exchange Act. Because Kalshi operates a CFTC-regulated designated contract market, it said federal jurisdiction displaced Nevada’s gaming laws. The Ninth Circuit rejected that argument at the preliminary-injunction stage. It found that the contracts likely fell outside the applicable meaning of “swap” because they functioned as sports bets. The panel consequently rejected Kalshi’s express, conflict and field-preemption arguments.

📣 Circuit Judge Ryan Nelson wrote that “the CFTC is not a national gambling regulator.” The court said Kalshi’s broader interpretation lacked a limiting principle and did not fit the surrounding statutory framework. That prediction extends beyond the court’s direct holding. The opinion said Kalshi’s broad interpretation of “swap” “would raise concerns under the major-questions doctrine.” It did not hold that the doctrine categorically prevents the CFTC from regulating prediction markets.

Julian Assange has given a stark account of what he says unfolded after WikiLeaks published material that powerful institutions wanted buried. He says the CIA drew up plans to kidnap and assassinate him inside the Ecuadorian Embassy in London, authorized action against his European colleagues, and subjected those around him to theft, hacking, and the planting of false information.

Assange says the campaign did not stop with him. A CIA asset was permanently assigned to track his wife. Instructions were given to obtain DNA from his six-month-old son’s nappy. A baby’s diaper. That is the allegation he places on the record: an intelligence operation that reached into his family after WikiLeaks exposed files tied to Hillary Clinton, John Podesta, Barack Obama, and other figures who wanted the leaks contained.

The Clinton remark now resurfacing is the line attributed to her while officials hunted ways to cut off the cables and limit the damage: “Can’t we just drone this guy?” In that telling, WikiLeaks was not treated as journalism. Assange was treated as a problem to be removed.

The larger question attached to his account is familiar to anyone who watched the war on Donald Trump. If agencies and political operators would plan a kidnapping, hunt a wife, seek an infant’s DNA, and float a drone strike to stop exposure, why assume they would stop short of a fabricated Russia narrative, the silencing of Seth Rich, lawfare, bankruptcy schemes, or election interference when their grip on power was at risk?

Assange turns the story away from personalities. He says he was convicted by a foreign power for asking for, receiving, and publishing truthful information while he was in Europe. “The criminalization of news gathering activities is a threat to investigative journalism everywhere,” he warns. “Journalists should not be prosecuted for doing their jobs.
